title: The Romantic Sensibility
description: Feeling, nature, the sublime, the self

concepts.title: What Romanticism Was
concepts.contentHtml:
Romanticism was a literary, artistic, and intellectual movement that swept Europe and the Americas roughly 1790-1850. It was a reaction against the 18th-century Enlightenment's emphasis on reason, order, and classical decorum.

Where the Augustan poets prized wit, balance, and social observation, the Romantics prized intensity, originality, and the inner life. Where neoclassicism looked back to Greece and Rome for models, Romanticism looked to medieval, folk, exotic, and personal sources.

The movement had national variants — German Romanticism, English Romanticism, French Romanticism, American Transcendentalism — but shared a recognisable family of attitudes.

concepts.title: Feeling and the Self
concepts.contentHtml:
The central Romantic move was to make individual feeling — and the individual self that has those feelings — the primary subject of serious literature.

Wordsworth's famous formulation in the 1800 Preface to Lyrical Ballads: poetry is 'the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings... recollected in tranquillity.' The poet's emotional life, observed and refined, becomes the material of the poem.

This was new. Earlier poetry had subjects — heroic action, religious meditation, moral satire, pastoral scene. Romantic poetry made the poet's own consciousness the subject. The autobiographical lyric in its modern form begins here.

concepts.title: Nature
concepts.contentHtml:
Romantic poetry put nature at the centre — not as decorative backdrop but as a moral and spiritual force.

Wordsworth's Lake District, Coleridge's Quantocks, Shelley's Alpine peaks, Byron's Mediterranean coasts — landscape becomes the place where the self meets something larger. Nature instructs. Nature consoles. Nature, encountered with sufficient receptivity, makes the self more real.

The political dimension matters. Industrialisation was transforming European landscapes. Romantic nature poetry was, in part, a protest against that transformation — defending what was being lost.

concepts.title: The Sublime
concepts.contentHtml:
The sublime was Romanticism's distinctive aesthetic category. Edmund Burke's A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757) provided the theoretical basis. Kant developed it in his Critique of Judgment (1790).

The sublime is what overwhelms the mind: vast mountains, raging storms, the night sky, ruins, anything immense and terrible. Confronted with the sublime, the self feels its own smallness — and then, paradoxically, its own grandeur in being able to register that smallness.

Romantic poetry seeks the sublime constantly. Shelley's Mont Blanc, Coleridge's chasms in 'Kubla Khan,' Wordsworth's Snowdon ascent — all are sublime encounters.

concepts.title: Imagination
concepts.contentHtml:
The Romantic imagination was not mere fancy. Coleridge in his Biographia Literaria (1817) distinguished primary imagination (the active perceiving mind), secondary imagination (the artist's shaping power), and fancy (mere recombination of images).

The imagination was creative — even, in Coleridge's most extreme formulation, godlike. The poet imagining is reenacting on a small scale what the divine creator does on a large one.

This high view of imagination set Romantic poetics against Enlightenment rationalism. Reason analyses; imagination creates. Reason categorises; imagination synthesises. The poet, in this view, is not a craftsman but a kind of seer.

title: English Romantics I — Wordsworth & Coleridge
description: Lyrical Ballads and the everyday raised

concepts.title: Lyrical Ballads
concepts.contentHtml:
Lyrical Ballads (1798) — a small anonymous volume by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge — is the conventional starting point of English Romanticism.

The book mixed Wordsworth's plain-style poems of rural life with Coleridge's supernatural ballad The Rime of the Ancient Mariner. The combination was deliberate: Wordsworth would treat ordinary subjects with imaginative intensity; Coleridge would treat extraordinary subjects with psychological credibility.

The 1800 second edition added Wordsworth's famous Preface — a manifesto for the new poetry. Plain language ('a selection of language really used by men'), rural subjects, emotional truth. The Preface remains the central document of English Romantic theory.

concepts.title: Wordsworth
concepts.contentHtml:
William Wordsworth (1770-1850) is the central English Romantic. His themes — nature, memory, the growth of the mind — defined the movement.

Major works: Lyrical Ballads (1798/1800), the great Ode 'Intimations of Immortality' (1804), The Prelude (composed 1798-1850, published posthumously), the sonnets, the meditative blank-verse poems including 'Tintern Abbey' and 'Resolution and Independence'.

The Prelude is his largest work — a 14-book autobiographical epic on the growth of the poetic mind. He revised it across his entire life. The 1805 version is the freshest; the 1850 version is more polished.

concepts.title: Coleridge
concepts.contentHtml:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772-1834) was Wordsworth's friend, collaborator, and antithesis. Where Wordsworth was steady and slow-moving, Coleridge was brilliant, restless, opium-addicted, perpetually unfinished.

The major poems: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner (1798), Christabel (begun 1797, never finished), Kubla Khan (1797, fragmentary), the conversation poems including 'Frost at Midnight' and 'This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison.'

His prose is equally important. Biographia Literaria (1817) is the central work of English Romantic criticism. The lectures on Shakespeare reshaped Shakespearean criticism for the 19th century.

concepts.title: Tintern Abbey
concepts.contentHtml:
'Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey' (1798) is one of the central English Romantic poems. Wordsworth at 28, revisiting the Wye Valley after five years, meditates on what nature and memory have done for him.

The structure: present scene, past memory, the gift of those memories during the absent years, and a turn to his sister Dorothy at the end — projecting onto her future the same gift he has received.

Key passages: 'a sense sublime / Of something far more deeply interfused, / Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, / And the round ocean and the living air...'

The poem demonstrates the Romantic mode at full power: meditative blank verse, the speaking self at the centre, nature as moral instructor, memory as redemptive.

concepts.title: After Lyrical Ballads
concepts.contentHtml:
The friendship between Wordsworth and Coleridge cooled by 1810. Coleridge's opium addiction worsened; his philosophical interests diverged from Wordsworth's poetic ones; the two men quarrelled and reconciled but never fully recovered the early intensity.

Wordsworth lived to 80, becoming a Tory and Poet Laureate, his radical youth long behind him. The early masterpieces remained the major work; later poetry was more diffuse.

Coleridge died at 62. His prose work continued through his later life — the lectures, the philosophical and theological writings, the table talk. The poetry largely stopped after 1802.

Together they had reshaped what English poetry could do. Every poet writing afterward worked in their shadow.

title: English Romantics II — Byron, Shelley, Keats

concepts.title: The Second Generation
concepts.contentHtml:
The second generation of English Romantics — Byron, Shelley, Keats — were a decade or two younger than Wordsworth and Coleridge. They were also more politically radical, more openly transgressive, and all three died young.

Keats died at 25 of tuberculosis in 1821. Shelley drowned at 29 in 1822. Byron died at 36 of fever in 1824 while supporting the Greek war of independence.

The deaths in close succession produced a powerful image of Romantic genius — burning bright and dying young. The image has been distorting ever since.

concepts.title: Byron
concepts.contentHtml:
George Gordon, Lord Byron (1788-1824) was the most famous poet of his time and one of the most famous men in Europe.

Major works: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage (1812-1818), Don Juan (1819-1824, unfinished at his death), the Oriental tales, the closet drama Manfred (1817).

Byron invented the Byronic hero — moody, brilliant, world-weary, sexually magnetic, morally ambiguous. The character type has run through Heathcliff, Mr Rochester, Edmond Dantès, and a thousand others.

Don Juan is his masterpiece — a comic epic in ottava rima, satirical, digressive, encyclopedic. Goethe called it 'a work of boundless genius.'

concepts.title: Shelley
concepts.contentHtml:
Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792-1822) was the most politically radical of the major Romantics. Atheist, vegetarian, free-love advocate, supporter of revolution. Expelled from Oxford for publishing The Necessity of Atheism.

Major works: Prometheus Unbound (1820), Adonais (1821, on Keats's death), The Mask of Anarchy (1819, on the Peterloo massacre), the Defence of Poetry (1821, posthumous).

His shorter lyrics — 'Ode to the West Wind,' 'To a Skylark,' 'Ozymandias,' 'When the lamp is shattered' — are among the most quoted poems in English.

The famous closing of A Defence of Poetry: 'Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world.'

concepts.title: Keats
concepts.contentHtml:
John Keats (1795-1821) is now the second-generation Romantic most consistently celebrated. Trained as a surgeon, dropped medicine for poetry. Wrote almost all his major work between 1818 and 1820.

Major poems: the great odes ('Ode to a Nightingale,' 'Ode on a Grecian Urn,' 'To Autumn,' 'Ode on Melancholy,' 'Ode to Psyche,' all 1819), The Eve of St Agnes (1819), Hyperion and The Fall of Hyperion (unfinished epics), the late sonnets.

Keats's distinctive ideas: negative capability (the capacity to remain in 'uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason'), the 'chameleon poet' (without identity of his own), beauty as truth.

concepts.title: The Women Romantics
concepts.contentHtml:
The traditional canon of English Romantic poetry — Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley, Keats — is entirely male. Recent scholarship has expanded the picture.

Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) is now read as a major Romantic work. Her novels The Last Man (1826) and Mathilda (written 1819, published 1959) are also significant.

Felicia Hemans and Letitia Landon were the most popular poets of the 1820s and 1830s — outsold the male canonical Romantics in their lifetimes. Their reputations collapsed in the 20th century, recovered by feminist scholarship.

Charlotte Smith's Elegiac Sonnets (1784) helped revive the sonnet form. Mary Robinson wrote major Romantic lyrics. Dorothy Wordsworth's journals are now read alongside her brother's poems.

concepts.title: German Romanticism
concepts.contentHtml:
German Romanticism began earlier than English — by the 1790s — and ran on a different theoretical track. The Jena circle around the brothers August and Friedrich Schlegel made German Romanticism the most philosophically self-conscious of the national movements.

Key figures: the Schlegel brothers, Novalis (Friedrich von Hardenberg), Tieck, E. T. A. Hoffmann. Their journal Athenäum (1798-1800) carried the programme.

The German romantic novel — Heinrich von Ofterdingen, the Hoffmann tales — leaned into the supernatural, the fragmentary, the philosophically suggestive. Hoffmann's tales of doubles, automata, and disturbed psyches influenced Poe and the entire 19th-century gothic tradition.

concepts.title: Goethe
concepts.contentHtml:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749-1832) sits at the boundary between Enlightenment, Sturm und Drang, classicism, and Romanticism. He outlived three literary movements.

Major works: The Sorrows of Young Werther (1774, the Sturm und Drang novel that made him famous across Europe), the Wilhelm Meister novels (1795-1829, the Bildungsroman's central early example), Faust Part 1 (1808) and Part 2 (1832, posthumous).

Faust is his masterpiece — a verse drama of immense scope, treating ambition, knowledge, love, and damnation across two parts written over sixty years. Part 2 is one of the strangest major works in European literature.

concepts.title: French Romanticism
concepts.contentHtml:
French Romanticism arrived later than German or English — really not until the 1820s — and was always partly a reaction against entrenched French classicism.

Victor Hugo (1802-1885) was the central figure. The 1830 premiere of his play Hernani — with its violation of classical theatrical rules — was the famous battle that announced French Romanticism's arrival.

Hugo's range was enormous: lyric poetry (Les Contemplations, 1856), novels (The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, 1831; Les Misérables, 1862), drama, political essays, exile pamphlets.

Other French Romantics: Lamartine, Vigny, Musset, Nerval — and Chateaubriand, who anticipated the movement in the 1800s.

concepts.title: Russian Romanticism
concepts.contentHtml:
Russian literary culture reached maturity in the Romantic period.

Alexander Pushkin (1799-1837) is the central figure — Russia's national poet. Eugene Onegin (1825-1832), a verse novel in 'Onegin stanzas,' is his masterpiece. The Tatiana-Onegin-Lensky triangle, the rural-urban contrast, the speaking authorial voice — all later Russian fiction grows from this.

Pushkin also wrote Boris Godunov, the prose Tales of Belkin, The Bronze Horseman, and many lyrics. Killed at 37 in a duel.

Mikhail Lermontov (1814-1841) was the next major poet — also dead in a duel, also at a young age. His novel A Hero of Our Time (1840) is the first major Russian psychological novel.

concepts.title: Romantic Nationalism
concepts.contentHtml:
Across Europe, Romanticism intersected powerfully with nationalism. The collection of folk tales, ballads, and legends became part of nation-building projects.

The Brothers Grimm in Germany collected the tales now known by their name (1812-1815). Their work was political — establishing a German cultural identity prior to and beneath state structures.

Similar projects across Europe: Walter Scott's Border ballads in Scotland, Karadžić's Serbian folk poetry, the Finnish Kalevala compiled by Lönnrot (1835).

Romanticism and nationalism are linked through to today. Almost every modern European national identity has Romantic literary foundations — a poet, a folk-tale collection, a novelist who 'speaks for the nation.'

concepts.title: The American Renaissance
concepts.contentHtml:
F. O. Matthiessen's American Renaissance (1941) named the extraordinary literary flowering of the 1840s and 1850s. In about fifteen years, the United States produced Emerson's essays, Thoreau's Walden, Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter, Melville's Moby-Dick, Whitman's Leaves of Grass, and the major work of Poe and Dickinson.

The American Renaissance was American Romanticism. Its concerns — nature, the self, the symbolic, the metaphysical — were Romantic concerns inflected by specifically American conditions.

concepts.title: Emerson and Transcendentalism
concepts.contentHtml:
Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803-1882) was the central American Romantic thinker. Transcendentalism — the New England movement he led — held that intuitive perception of moral and spiritual truth was available directly to every individual, beneath and beyond the structures of religion and society.

Major essays: 'Self-Reliance' (1841), 'The American Scholar' (1837), 'Nature' (1836), 'Experience' (1844), 'The Poet' (1844).

Emerson's prose — aphoristic, paradoxical, oracular — became the central American intellectual voice of the 19th century. Whitman, Thoreau, Dickinson, William James, John Dewey all carry his influence.

concepts.title: Thoreau
concepts.contentHtml:
Henry David Thoreau (1817-1862) was Emerson's most famous follower and most original divergent. Walden (1854) records his two years living in a cabin at Walden Pond — pursuing the experiment of seeing what was essential.

Walden's mode is part natural history, part philosophical meditation, part economic argument, part spiritual autobiography. The famous opening: 'I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life...'

'Civil Disobedience' (1849) made Thoreau a political figure. The essay's argument for non-violent resistance to unjust government influenced Tolstoy, Gandhi, and Martin Luther King Jr.

concepts.title: Hawthorne and Melville
concepts.contentHtml:
Nathaniel Hawthorne (1804-1864) wrote a darker American Romanticism. The Puritan past, ancestral guilt, hidden sin, the moral ambiguity of every action.

Major works: The Scarlet Letter (1850), The House of the Seven Gables (1851), the tales (Twice-Told Tales, Mosses from an Old Manse).

Herman Melville (1819-1891) was Hawthorne's friend and acolyte. Moby-Dick (1851), dedicated to Hawthorne, is now considered the great American novel — a metaphysical sea narrative of immense ambition. It sold 3,200 copies in his lifetime. Recovery began in the 1920s.

Melville's late short fiction (Bartleby, Benito Cereno, Billy Budd) and his poetry are now also recognised as major.

concepts.title: Poe, Whitman, Dickinson
concepts.contentHtml:
Edgar Allan Poe (1809-1849) was American Romanticism's master of the gothic and the analytical. The horror tales ('The Fall of the House of Usher,' 'The Tell-Tale Heart,' 'The Cask of Amontillado'); the detective stories that invented the genre ('The Murders in the Rue Morgue'); the poems ('The Raven,' 'Annabel Lee'); the criticism ('The Philosophy of Composition'). Influence on French Symbolism via Baudelaire's translations was foundational.

Walt Whitman's Leaves of Grass (first edition 1855, expanded over his life) invented modern American free verse. The expansive, cataloguing, erotic, democratic voice — first-person and oceanic — has shaped American poetry ever since.

Emily Dickinson (1830-1886) wrote nearly 1,800 poems, almost none published in her lifetime. Compressed, slant-rhyming, philosophically charged. Now considered alongside Whitman as American poetry's central 19th-century figure.
